title: See and Be Seen
summary: Riders should scan 10 to 15 seconds ahead along their path of travel.
Drivers involved in motorcycle crashes most often say they did not see the rider; a motorcycle's small size also makes it seem farther away and slower than it really is.
Most motorcycle crashes happen in daylight, so bright clothing (orange, red, yellow, green) and reflective tape or a reflective vest improve visibility.
Keeping the headlight on at all times is the best way to be noticed; in daylight it makes a motorcycle twice as noticeable to oncoming drivers, and using high beam in daytime adds visibility.
A motorcycle brake light is less noticeable than a car's, so flash it before slowing or stopping, especially when being tailgated.
Know the hand signals: left arm straight out for a left turn, forearm bent upward for a right turn, and arm angled downward for slowing or stopping.
Turn signals tell others your intentions and make you more visible; use them for every lane change even when no one seems to be around, and always cancel them afterward.
Use the horn when another vehicle may be moving into your lane, but be ready to stop or swerve as well.
Each lane offers three paths of travel; choose a position that keeps you out of blind spots and visible in the mirrors of vehicles ahead, and pass through blind spots quickly.
SPIDER stands for Scan, Predict, Identify, Decide, Execute, Rely.
In the city look one-half to one full block ahead; on the highway look as far ahead as you safely can, and watch for oil and gravel on curves and ramps.
Check mirrors every few seconds, use a head check before changing lanes, and remember convex mirrors make vehicles behind seem farther away than they are; intersections are the greatest danger.

questions.q: How far ahead along your path of travel should you scan?
questions.explanation: The manual lists scanning 10 to 15 seconds ahead as one of the ways to reduce your chance of a crash.

questions.q: In crashes involving motorcycles, what do other drivers most often cite as the leading cause?
options: They did not see the rider
questions.explanation: Drivers frequently say a lack of rider visibility was the main cause of the crash.

questions.q: Because of a motorcycle's small size, other drivers may misjudge it. How?
options: It seems closer and faster than it is
It seems farther away and slower than it is
It seems closer but slower than it is
Its size has no effect on how drivers judge it
questions.explanation: Smaller vehicles appear more distant and slower-moving than they really are, so drivers can misjudge a rider's distance and speed.

questions.q: When do most accidents involving motorcycles happen?
questions.explanation: The manual states that most motorcycle crashes occur in daylight, which is why bright clothing matters even during the day.

questions.q: If you choose not to wear brightly colored clothing, what does the manual suggest?
options: Ride only on roads with light traffic
questions.explanation: A reflective vest is recommended as a way to alert drivers to your presence when you are not wearing bright colors.

questions.q: What is the best way to alert other drivers to your presence on a motorcycle?
options: Ride in the left part of the lane
Keep your headlight on at all times
questions.explanation: Keeping the headlight on at all times is described as the best way to make drivers aware of you.

questions.q: According to research cited in the manual, how much more noticeable is a motorcycle with its headlight on during daylight?
questions.explanation: Research shows a daytime headlight makes a motorcycle twice as noticeable to oncoming drivers.

questions.q: When is it especially important to flash your brake light before slowing?
options: When the road ahead is clear
When you are being followed too closely
questions.explanation: A tailgater may be focused only on your motorcycle and unaware of hazards ahead, so flashing the brake light warns them you are slowing.

questions.q: Which hand signal indicates a left turn?
questions.explanation: The manual's illustration shows a left turn signaled with the left arm held straight out horizontally.

questions.q: Should you use your turn signal when changing lanes if no other vehicles seem to be around?
options: No, signals are only needed when vehicles are nearby
questions.explanation: The manual recommends always signaling a lane change, even when no vehicle may be present.

questions.q: Why is a turn signal that is left blinking dangerous?
options: A driver may pull into your path expecting you to turn
It is a moving violation in every case
questions.explanation: An uncanceled signal can lead a driver to expect your turn and move into your path, so check your instrument panel after turning.

questions.q: A driver in the next lane is quickly approaching another vehicle and may pull into your lane. Besides being ready to use your horn, what should you be prepared to do?
options: Speed up to block the driver
Move onto the shoulder and stop
Be ready to stop or swerve
Flash your headlight and hold your speed
questions.explanation: The manual says the horn helps in this situation, but the rider should also be ready to stop or swerve away from danger.

questions.q: How many distinct paths of travel does each marked traffic lane give a motorcycle rider?
questions.explanation: Each marked lane offers a rider three paths of travel for choosing a visible position.

questions.q: When passing another vehicle, how should you handle the driver's blind spot?
options: Get through it as quickly as possible
Stay in it until the driver signals
Slow down to match the vehicle's speed
Sound your horn and ride alongside
questions.explanation: Riders should avoid lingering in blind spots; decide early, approach carefully, and once alongside speed up and pass quickly.

questions.q: In the SPIDER process, what does the "D" stand for?
questions.explanation: SPIDER stands for Scan, Predict, Identify, Decide, Execute, and Rely.

questions.q: When riding in the city, how far ahead should you look?
options: As far as the next traffic light only
questions.explanation: The manual recommends looking one-half block to one full block ahead in city riding.

questions.q: Where should you pay particular attention for oil and gravel on the road surface?
questions.explanation: Curves and ramps are singled out as places where oil and gravel tend to collect.

questions.q: How do convex motorcycle mirrors affect what you see behind you?
options: Objects look closer than they are
Objects look larger than they are
They have no effect on apparent distance
Objects look farther away than they are
questions.explanation: Convex mirrors show more of the road behind but make vehicles appear more distant, so practice judging distance with them.

questions.q: Before changing lanes, what should a responsible rider do in addition to checking mirrors?
options: Turn the head to check for vehicles
questions.explanation: The manual says to include a head turn to visually check for vehicles approaching or trying to pass before a lane change.

questions.q: According to the manual, which location poses the greatest danger to a motorcycle rider?
questions.explanation: Intersections, meaning any place traffic may cross your path, are described as the greatest danger.
